title: Refactor runtime plugin registry to support per-model kernel manifests and atomic activation
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem: the current runtime plugin registry resolves kernels globally and performs best-effort fallbacks at startup. This causes non-deterministic kernel selection for mixed fleets and complicated rollback paths when a kernel ABI change is introduced. We also lack a per-model manifest to express supported kernel artifacts (CUTLASS variant, Triton plugin version, quant profile) which makes canarying model-level kernel upgrades fragile.

Goal: refactor the runtime plugin registry to: (1) accept and validate a per-model kernel manifest bundled with model artifacts; (2) support atomic activation of signed kernel bundles and deterministic fallback order; (3) expose a simple compatibility check API for the scheduler/allocator and the console to reason about runtime compatibility; (4) add telemetry and CI gates to detect symbol-level mismatches early.

Scope: runtime registry refactor in C++ core + small control-plane wiring in the admissions/loader path, manifest schema design, CI job to build and sign kernel bundles, and a canary rollout plan that exercises model-level pinning. This ticket covers the refactor and integration testing; follow-ups will implement rollout dashboards and automated rollback playbooks.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime can read a per-model kernel manifest (JSON) that lists kernel artifacts with checksums and ABI tags
Registry can atomically activate a signed kernel bundle and report success/failure without partial state exposure
Deterministic fallback order applied when preferred kernel is unavailable, with clear telemetry events emitted
Scheduler can query manifest compatibility and reject incompatible placements during admission
End-to-end CI builds kernel bundles, signs them, and runs the model smoke suite in a canary pool
Rollout plan documented with emergency rollback steps and a feature-flag guarded activation
tasks: Design manifest schema (fields: artifact_name, arch, cuda_min, triton_version, cutlass_variant, checksum, signature_meta)
Add parser and validator for manifest to runtime loader (C++), return rich error codes for console
Implement atomic swap + verification: download -> verify signature -> stage temp -> fsync -> atomic rename
Extend plugin registry map to index by model_id -> active_kernel_manifest (allow side-by-side models)
Add compatibility-check RPC to allocator/placement service and wire to admission flow
Create CI pipeline: build kernel bundles, produce signed artifacts, run canary smoke tests (perf + correctness)
Write unit + integration tests including synthetic heterogenous GPU host matrix
Prepare rollout runbook and safety toggles (feature flag + max-failure-rate gate)
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: signature verification adds latency to cold activation. Mitigation: perform async verification and warm prefetch for hot models; measure and cap extra latency in canary.
Risk: incorrect manifest schema could block model deployments. Mitigation: provide backwards-compatible loader that accepts legacy models and logs deprecation warnings for two cycles.
Risk: storage corruption during atomic swap. Mitigation: use tempfile + fsync pattern and store activation journal for safety and rollback.
Risk: increased disk footprint for side-by-side kernel bundles. Mitigation: add dedupe by checksum and optional shared-store index in follow-up ticket.
benchmarks_and_metrics: Perf baseline: current cold-start median activation time = 520ms (measured on p4d-like nodes)
Target: initial cold activation <= 650ms with signed verification step; subsequent activations should be unchanged
Desired throughput effect: no more than 3% regression at 99th percentile under mixed-model traffic; we expect ~6-12% throughput improvement where kernel preloads reduce probe jitter
Telemetry: surface activation success rate, fallback counts, symbol_mismatch_count, canary model error-rate vs baseline
design_notes_and_tradeoffs: We considered a centralized kernel catalog approach. Trade-off: simplifies global upgrades but couples models to a single upgrade domain and makes rollback harder. Chosen per-model manifests allow safer canaries and model-scoped rollbacks.
Manifest signing: leverage existing KMS/HSM keys used by private deployments to sign bundles. Alternative (unsigned) is faster but introduces security/compliance risks for enterprise customers.
Atomic activation implemented via filesystem rename to avoid complex distributed coordination; this keeps runtime simple and debuggable.
We deliberately avoid embedding large vendor blobs in the model archive; instead we reference kernel bundle artifact URLs with checksums to allow shared caching in the infra layer.
Backward compatibility: runtime will accept old-style global-only plugins for one release cycle with deprecation telemetry.
ci_and_release_plan: Create pipeline job runtime/kernel-bundle-build that produces artifacts and uploads to internal CDN (artifact hash in manifest)
Add gating job runtime/manifest-compat-check that runs symbol-level diff between current lib and candidate bundles
Rollout in phases: local dev -> staging (10% traffic) -> canary pool (1-3 nodes) -> gradual increase with monitoring gates
Release flag: runtime-1.19.feature.per_model_manifests; enable default off for Hosted, on for internal staging
Backout: feature flag off + registry can force-use global fallback bundle; documented in runbook
qa_plan: Integration test harness that simulates heterogeneous hosts (different CUDA, driver, GPU families) and validates manifest resolution
System tests: forced symbol mismatch scenarios produce clear error logs and do not crash the process
Performance test: measure cold-start and 99p latency across mixed-model traffic before/after change
Chaos test: simulate partial artifact corruption and verify atomic activation and journaled rollback
Security QA: verify signature verification handles revoked keys and malformed manifests gracefully
